newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HORSE RACING-HK HIT BY MAJOR RACE-FIXING SCANDAL.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-HK HIT BY MAJOR RACE-FIXING SCANDAL.

text.p: Hong Kong horse-racing, one of the territory's richest businesses, was hit by its biggest scandal on Monday as 37 people, including jockeys and trainers, were arrested in a probe on race fixing.

The British colony's graft-fighting body, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), announced the arrests after a dramatic swoop by 220 ICAC officers during a meeting at Shatin racecourse in Hong Kong's New Territories on Sunday.
The ICAC said late on Monday it had released six of the 37 on bail, while the other 31 were still being questioned.
The detained persons, the ICAC said, included two trainers, five jockeys and three staff of the Hong Kong Jockey Club, which has a monopoly on horseracing and gaming in the territory.
The ICAC also raided 55 premises on Sunday, including two suspected of being illegal bookmaking operations, it said.
The commission, which has extensive powers, said it was probing charges jockeys and trainers were "corruptly involved with illegal bookmakers in syndicated horse race fixing".
The ICAC said the raids were the result of a probe following a tipoff from the Jockey Club's security department.
The scandal has been likened to a 1986 swoop on a "Shanghai Syndicate" that controlled horses, jockeys and trainers in the biggest previous scandal to engulf the colony's racing scene.
This territory of 6.4 million people is one of two major horse-racing centres in Asia -- the other is Japan.

Hong Kong is among the world's liveliest racing centres. Top jockeys who regularly ride here include Irishman Mick Kinane, Frenchmen Eric St Martin and Eric Legrix and South Africans Basil Marcus and Pierre Strydom. Trainers include France's Patrick Biancone and Australians John Moore and David Hayes.
As the only legal outlet for a flutter on the horses, the races generate billions of dollars in taxes and for charity.
Betting turnover in the 1995/96 season was HK$80.6 billion (US$11 billion), believed the highest per capita in the world, and well above some of the territory's biggest companies.
Conglomerate Swire Pacific Ltd, for example, last week reported turnover of HK$38.356 billion for 1996.

On Monday, officers whisked suspects in cars and vans in and out of the ICAC building in the heart of Hong Kong's commercial hub, whizzing past an army of journalists. It is ICAC policy not to identify anyone it is investigating.
Australian jockey Damien Oliver, whose successes include the coveted Melbourne Cup, was seen entering ICAC headquarters, but he declined to tell reporters the reason for his visit.
ICAC officers ferried black plastic bags into the building, but the office gave no details what they contained.
ICAC spokeswoman Lisa Li told Reuters no charges had yet been laid against anyone. Arrested persons can be held for 48 hours before being charged.
A Jockey Club spokesman said the club was "working closely with the ICAC" on the case but witheld further comment.
Under legal reporting curbs, media have to confine reports about corruption cases under ICAC investigation to details which the commission itself issues.
Those detained were believed to include some of the cream of the British colony's international horseracing set.
"We will not disclose names of the people arrested. They will be kept confidential," Li said.
She declined to comment on the accuracy of local newspaper reports identifying prominent local and international trainers and jockeys as being among those netted in the swoop.
The Jockey Club is one of Hong Kong's most venerable institutions -- the first race was run in 1841 shortly after a naval shore patrol planted the colonial British flag here.
Hong Kong reverts to China in July, with many in the colony, fearing an upsurge in corruption under the influence of the mainland, where graft has run rife in recent years.
Robin Parke, a racing expert for the English-language daily South China Morning Post, told Reuters the only comparable scandal was the 1986 Shanghai Syndicate incident.
If the latest investigation took a similar course to the 1986 investigation, some of those arrested could be charged with conspiring to cheat the public at gambling, Parke said.
They could also face Jockey Club penalties, he said.

The immensely influential and wealthy Jockey Club has always been sensitive to suggestions of malpractice in view of the vast sums of money which Hong Kong punters pour into races at Happy Valley and the ultra-modern track at Shatin.
In October it banned two Hong Kong jockeys from riding for nine months for "stopping their horses running on their merits" in a race at Happy Valley in the centre of Hong Kong island.
